plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a two-lens telescope system consisting of a convex objective lens (lens 1, on the left) and a concave eyepiece lens (lens 2, on the right), with the distances f1 and f2 indicated by horizontal brackets beneath the optical axis. Two parallel input rays enter from the left at a small angle δᵢ relative to the optical axis; lens 1 bends them toward the objective focal point to the right of lens 2, and lens 2 then diverges the rays so they exit as a parallel bundle at a larger angle δₒ. The blue vertical marker d shows the offset of the shared focal point from the optical axis in the shown Galilean afocal geometry, where the objective focal point aligns with the eyepiece focal point. This figure demonstrates how a Galilean-style telescope achieves angular magnification equal to the ratio f1/f2 by manipulating ray angles through the two-lens arrangement.

interactionPlan.concept: A Galilean telescope (convex objective + concave eyepiece) turns an input ray angle δᵢ into a larger output angle δₒ with magnification exactly f₁/f₂, but only when the lenses are separated by f₁ − f₂ so they share a focal point (the afocal condition).

interactions.label: Objective focal length f₁
interactions.teaches: Lengthening f₁ makes the objective converge the rays more gently, so for the same input angle the shared focal point lands at a larger offset d — and the angular magnification grows in direct proportion to f₁.

interactions.label: Eyepiece focal length f₂
interactions.teaches: Shrinking f₂ makes the eyepiece re-collimate the converging rays into a steeper exit angle, so magnification grows as f₂ shrinks — what matters is the ratio f₁/f₂, not either focal length alone.

Dragging the incoming parallel-ray bundle to a new tilt δᵢ shows the exit bundle tilting in exact proportion — δₒ/δᵢ stays pinned at f₁/f₂ regardless of δᵢ, revealing the telescope as a linear angle amplifier, not a device tuned to one input angle.

Dragging the eyepiece along the axis away from the shared-focus separation f₁ − f₂ makes the exit bundle visibly converge or diverge instead of staying parallel, and the focal-point marker d no longer lines up with the eyepiece — the simple magnification law exists only in the afocal configuration.

demo_steps.title: Afocal geometry
demo_steps.narration: Lens 1 sits f₁ from the shared focal point and lens 2 sits f₂ from it, so the lens separation is f₁ − f₂ and both lenses share one focal point, offset d below the axis. Parallel rays entering at angle δᵢ are steered through that shared focus.

demo_steps.title: Angle in, angle out
demo_steps.narration: Drag the incoming ray bundle to change δᵢ: the exit bundle stays parallel and its angle δₒ tracks δᵢ in fixed proportion. Watch the readout — δₒ/δᵢ stays pinned at f₁/f₂ = 4 no matter how you tilt the input.

demo_steps.title: Magnification is a ratio
demo_steps.narration: Move the sliders: increasing f₁ or decreasing f₂ steepens the exit angle and the readout updates in real time, while lens 2 automatically re-seats itself at separation f₁ − f₂ so the system stays afocal throughout.

demo_steps.title: Break the afocal condition
demo_steps.narration: Now drag lens 2 along the axis away from its afocal seat: the exit bundle is no longer parallel — it converges or diverges — and the blue focal-point marker d sits at a mismatch from the eyepiece. The clean law δₒ/δᵢ = f₁/f₂ holds only at the shared-focus separation.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The objective converts input angle into focal-plane offset (d ≈ f₁·δᵢ) and the eyepiece converts that offset back into angle (δₒ ≈ d/f₂), so the angular magnification is exactly f₁/f₂ — provided the two lenses share a focal point.

authoredContext: A small change in the input ray angle gives a larger change in the output ray angle. The magnification of the telescope is the ratio, $M$, of the angular deviation of an output ray, $\delta_o$, to the angular deviation of an input ray, $\delta_i$.  Writing the focal point offset, $d$, in terms of the rays passing through the centers of lenses 1 and 2 gives the relation, $M = f_1/f_2$, where $f_1$ and $f_2$ are the respective ray focal lengths.
